newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian rebels insist Berisha must go.
newsitem.headline: Albanian rebels insist Berisha must go.

text.p: Albanian rebels on Tuesday stood by demands that President Sali Berisha, blamed for losses from failed investment schemes, must quit before they would surrender their weapons.

Rebel leaders, speaking after meeting Greek Deputy Foreign Minister Yannos Kranidiotis in this southern town, said they had also called on the government of Prime Minister Bashkim Fino to cut all ties with Berisha.
The rebel leader in Gjirokaster, former army general Agim Ghozita, told Reuters Television the southern rebels were giving Berisha until March 20 to quit or they would elect their own government.

He said rebels wanted to work with Fino but this would not be possible if he continued to cooperate with the president. Berisha named Fino, an opposition Socialist, prime minister in March in a desperate bid to cling to power.
Ghozita said the rebels wanted a political and not a military solution to the crisis which has racked Albania for three weeks.

If Berisha, elected by parliament to a fresh five-year term this month, did not resign, rebels and other political forces in the south would elect their own presidential council within the next few days to challenge him directly.

Rebels blame Berisha for the collapse of popular investment schemes in January, which cost thousands of Albanians their life savings, and accuse his right-wing Democratic Party of profiting from the get-rich-quick scams.
Berisha agreed to hold national elections by June and said he would quit if his Democratic Party lost, but this has failed to satisfy rebels who want him out now.
Fino, a native of Gjirokaster, is expected to visit the town on Wednesday to talk to rebel leaders.
Kranidiotis toured the Albanian border region and met rebel leaders in Gjirokaster.

"Greece will assist as much as possible towards a political solution without use of force and violence," he said. "Of course I am here to underline our concern and interest for the safety of the rights of the Greek community in Albania."
After meeting rebels, he said: "The common denominator in their views is that Berisha should quit."
Kranidiotis also visited the ethnic Greek village of Dervican, south of Gjirokaster, where he was greeted with cheers and applause.
Greece was concerned about the safety of the Greek minority, estimated by Athens at 80,000-120,000 in the south, he said.
The Greek goverenment said on Tuesday it was ready to guarantee a loan to Albania to help cover losses from the pyramid schemes after the situation in the neighbouring country normalised.
